notes.bp: Vocal-fold vibration is physical motion that a microphone observes indirectly; ultrasound may measure the motion itself.
notes.wh: Ultrasound has spatial and temporal limits, and frequency estimates can alias when the voice is faster than acquisition.
notes.naive: Treat waveform pitch as the only description of vocal-fold motion.
notes.ap: Use M-mode ultrasound along the larynx and compare its fundamental-frequency estimate with simultaneous voice analysis.
notes.mech: Spatio-temporal maps of the fundamental and second harmonic are compared with median f0 from recordings.
notes.math: A linear fit gives f0-US = 0.997 f0-voice + 0.293 with correlation 0.999; differences are below 2 Hz in 92% of recordings.
notes.dots: The source/filter question becomes a sensing question: the vocal source can be observed through a different physical projection.
notes.ww: The paper reports close agreement and reveals temporal drift; four high-pitched recordings expose aliasing.
notes.limits: The 500-Hz rate, probe placement, healthy participants, and excluded aliased cases limit clinical and high-pitch claims.

notes.bp: When speech is inpainted, several completions may fit the observed context, so uncertainty is part of the missing-sound problem.
notes.wh: A single plausible waveform hides whether the missing content was determined by the evidence.
notes.naive: Return one deterministic reconstruction and treat residual error as the only uncertainty signal.
notes.ap: Use Neural Principal Probability Components to represent the posterior over possible inpaintings and compare it with dropout sampling.
notes.mech: NPPC predicts principal components of the conditional output distribution; traversing components produces alternative spectrograms and transcripts.
notes.math: NPPC is reported as 50x faster than 50-sample MC Dropout with slightly better reconstruction error.
notes.dots: The output is a distribution over repairs, not a single answer; uncertainty changes both sound and what ASR hears.
notes.ww: Principal directions change word identity and pitch; NPPC captures diverse outputs while matching or improving dropout error.
notes.limits: The data, posterior approximation, audio examples, and benchmark define the result; calibration and user decision rules remain unresolved.

notes.bp: A speech representation can encode phonetic and word information differently across languages and speaking styles.
notes.wh: Probe accuracy, downstream ASR, and corpus match can disagree, so one score cannot establish what a representation knows.
notes.naive: Use a multilingual representation as language-neutral and judge it by one WER.
notes.ap: Compare English, multilingual, and Dutch self-supervised models with linguistic probes and downstream Dutch ASR across read and conversational speech.
notes.mech: Hidden layers are probed for phonetic and lexical structure, then models are fine-tuned and evaluated on five Dutch test sets.
notes.math: The Dutch model WERs are 10.4 CGN-o, 65.6 IFADV, 15.4 MLS, 21.0 CV, and 25.2 N-Best; English is consistently worse.
notes.dots: Representation quality depends on language and pretraining domain: conversation-trained data helps conversational structure and recognition.
notes.ww: Language-specific pretraining yields lower WER, while probe and fine-tuning rankings need not coincide.
notes.limits: Models, Dutch corpora, probes, and fine-tuning limit generalization; decodability is not causal proof of ASR behavior.

notes.bp: Turn timing is jointly produced by two people; one speaker can wait differently with different partners and topics.
notes.wh: A model that sees only preceding words misses dyad-specific habits, common ground, and social coordination.
notes.naive: Predict a boundary from current-speaker features and treat talkers as independent.
notes.ap: Measure transition-floor offset across dyads and model individual, demographic, topic, and pair-specific effects hierarchically.
notes.mech: Spontaneous English dyads are analyzed by mixed models separating individual idiosyncrasy from dyad-specific interaction.
notes.math: Marginal R2 and random-effects comparisons show dyadic effects dominate the reported variation.
notes.dots: Turn-taking is interactional state, not merely a local acoustic event; the pair is a meaningful unit.
notes.ww: Sex and age have smaller effects while dyad variation most strongly shapes timing; TFO decreases across sampled lifespan.
notes.limits: English strangers, sparse older data, topic mix, and TFO limit familiar-relationship and full-dialogue claims.

notes.bp: Low-resource TTS can have correct content but unnatural acoustic detail, so postprocessing must improve naturalness without changing speech.
notes.wh: The target has little data, objective distances are listening proxies, and a postprocessor can improve one aspect while harming prosody.
notes.naive: Train a large TTS model directly on the small speaker set or add noise and assume naturalness follows.
notes.ap: Generate training examples from high-resource speakers and train GAN or consistency-flow postprocessors selected for low-resource targets.
notes.mech: Forward Tacotron features are refined by GAN and CFM postprocessors, then compared with listening and ranking tests.
notes.math: Proposed CFM reaches objective distance 0.27; listener scores are 79.8 proposed CFM and 74.8 proposed GAN versus reference 98.3.
notes.dots: Postprocessing separates generation from naturalness repair, but the metric must still be checked against listeners.
notes.ww: Both proposed postprocessors improve reported naturalness; the CFM gain over its standard version is not significant.
notes.limits: Two speakers, ground-truth prosody in part of evaluation, selected data, and reported tests limit arbitrary-voice claims.

notes.bp: Speaker verification must decide identity while content may be the same or different, without confusing lexical matching with speaker evidence.
notes.wh: Text-independent and text-dependent trials expose different shortcuts; a representation helping one can fail when phrase content changes.
notes.naive: Train separate systems for every language and treat verification as one undifferentiated score.
notes.ap: Use a unified self-supervised student for text validation and speaker verification, then evaluate tandem decisions across multilingual trials.
notes.mech: The student preserves lexical information for text validation while a speaker backend supplies identity evidence; DeepMine and VoxCeleb1 test both modes.
notes.math: English DeepMine TD-SV tandem EER is 3.46% versus 4.28% baseline; VoxCeleb1 TI-SV is 1.29% versus 0.49%, exposing a tradeoff.
notes.dots: Identity evidence is entangled with lexical content unless trial design forces separation.
notes.ww: The student improves reported text-dependent and DeepMine results but degrades VoxCeleb1 text-independent results relative to ReDimNet.
notes.limits: Datasets, languages, content, thresholds, and reported EERs bound the conclusion; open-set deployment is unestablished.

notes.bp: Code-switched speech alternates languages within an utterance, so recognition must switch language and script expectations without losing context.
notes.wh: Whisper behavior differs sharply on code-switched speech, especially across scripts; synthetic speech may add artifacts.
notes.naive: Train on monolingual data and expect multilingual modeling to interpolate automatically.
notes.ap: Build CS-FLEURS across 52 languages and 113 pairs, compare real and synthetic controls, and add synthetic code-switched training data.
notes.mech: The corpus controls pair and switching conditions; experiments compare CER, direct translation, script pairs, and augmented training.
notes.math: Distinct-script CER is about 3x same-script CER; synthetic training lowers reported seen CER 14.38 to 12.67 and unseen 29.62 to 27.77.
notes.dots: Cross-lingual recognition is a switching problem in language and writing system; data design determines the failure measured.
notes.ww: Code-switched ASR is over twice as errorful as monolingual speech, while synthetic training improves seen and unseen pairs.
notes.limits: Language pairs, synthetic voices, Whisper, CER, and controlled read speech limit natural-conversation claims.

notes.bp: A transcript can differ from reference words yet remain understandable, especially for disordered speech; evaluation must measure recoverable meaning.
notes.wh: WER and CER penalize harmless substitutions and can reward exact but unintelligible text.
notes.naive: Use WER as the universal speech-quality measure because it is easy to compute.
notes.ap: Fit a metric combining natural-language inference, semantic similarity, and phonetic similarity to human ratings of ASR outputs.
notes.mech: Five-fold regression learns weights from 100 transcript pairs rated by six annotators, then tests the combined score against held-out judgments.
notes.math: The combined metric correlates 0.890 with human judgments; weights are 0.40 NLI, 0.28 semantic, and 0.32 phonetic, with MSE 0.237.
notes.dots: A metric is a model of the human target: choosing the target changes which errors count as failures.
notes.ww: The integrated measure outperforms individual and traditional error measures in the reported SAP evaluation.
notes.limits: One dataset, six annotators, regression assumptions, and reported correlation limit other listeners, languages, and clinical decisions.
